analysis.one_liner: Phases out ozone-destroying CFCs and sets first carbon dioxide limits on power plants and cars.
analysis.headline: The bill got only one hearing in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, was never reported out or voted on, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have phased out chemicals that destroy the ozone layer (like CFCs and halons), put the first limits on carbon dioxide from power plants, new homes, and cars, and sharply tightened smog controls on vehicles and fuels. It was one of the first comprehensive climate bills in Congress. It never got a committee vote or a floor vote; the Senate committee it was sent to held a single hearing and let it die.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people: anyone breathing smog (tighter tailpipe and fuel standards), anyone at risk of skin cancer from ozone depletion (a full phase-out of CFCs and halons by 1996 with only narrow medical and appliance-servicing exceptions), and anyone exposed to coal-plant and vehicle pollution (first-ever carbon dioxide limits, stricter nitrogen oxide and hydrocarbon controls, ten-year/100,000-mile emissions warranties, and mandatory state inspection programs). It also empowered citizen lawsuits and set national goals of 50% nonpolluting energy by 2000 and 100% by 2050.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to smog and ozone depletion

how_it_helps.text: Would have phased out production of ozone-depleting chemicals to 5% of 1987 levels by 1994 and to zero (except medical uses) by 1996, with use bans by 1995/2000 and only a ten-year grace period for servicing existing household appliances like refrigerators and air conditioners.

Would have imposed the first carbon dioxide standards on fossil-fuel power plants (610 lbs per million BTU in 1991 falling to 280 by 2011) and on cars and light trucks (at least 10% below 1985 levels by 1991 rising to 75% by 2011), plus efficiency requirements for new home furnaces, air conditioners, and water heaters.

Would have cut smog-forming pollution with stricter tailpipe standards (0.25 g/mile hydrocarbons and 0.4 g/mile nitrogen oxides), banned engines requiring leaded gasoline after model year 1992, required onboard vapor recovery at the gas pump, capped diesel sulfur at 0.05%, and required every state to run vehicle inspection and maintenance programs.

Would have extended emissions warranties to ten years or 100,000 miles, required manufacturers to label warranty costs and recall vehicles with repeated defect patterns, and let citizens sue to enforce the law, with civil penalties up to $25,000 per day and criminal penalties for knowing violations.

Would have banned venting and flaring of methane after 1995, required landfills to control methane emissions, and set a national goal of 50% of U.S. energy from nonpolluting sources by 2000 and 100% by 2050, with a commission to develop inherently safe nuclear technology.

analysis.who_pays: Producers of ozone-depleting chemicals, coal-fired electric utilities (the carbon dioxide limits effectively priced out conventional coal generation), automakers (tighter standards, longer warranties, recall exposure), and oil refiners (low-sulfur diesel, summer gasoline vapor-pressure caps, oxygenated fuel mandates) would bear compliance costs, some of which would reach consumers through higher prices for cars, appliances, and electricity. Households also faced requirements to dispose of old refrigerators and air conditioners through licensed handlers who destroyed the chemicals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers, coal utilities, automakers, refiners

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs were real and would partly reach consumers: stricter tailpipe and fuel standards raise car and gasoline prices, and the carbon dioxide caps on power plants would force expensive retirements or retrofits of coal units, raising electricity prices.

The car carbon dioxide targets were far ahead of what Congress or regulators adopted at the time — a 75% cut from 1985 levels by 2011 — and the bill's deadlines (some effective within a year of passage) left little runway for industry adjustment.

The bill's disposal rules initially allowed only governmental entities to accept appliances containing listed chemicals for disposal, and its 99.999% destruction requirements added handling costs for households and businesses retiring equipment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes were large — ozone depletion meant higher skin-cancer rates, and smog and carbon pollution carried broad costs the bill would have cut — while the costs, though real, fell mostly on a few industries and only partly on consumers in the form of higher prices. The bill was sweeping and some deadlines were aggressive, arguably ahead of available technology for the vehicle carbon targets. Notably, its most urgent piece, the CFC phase-out, became law anyway within two years through the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which also adopted much of its smog and fuel program; the carbon dioxide limits did not, and comprehensive federal climate legislation stalled for decades afterward.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee it was sent to held one hearing and never voted to advance it, so it never reached the Senate floor and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on February 2, 1989, with one Republican cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The only action beyond referral was a Subcommittee on Environmental Protection hearing on May 19, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-120.
The committee never reported the bill, no committee or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers of ozone-depleting chemicals, coal-fired utilities, automakers, and oil refiners were better off because the bill died, since they avoided the phase-outs and emission caps. The public eventually got the CFC phase-out and much of the smog program through the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, but the bill's carbon dioxide limits went nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical, coal, auto, and oil producers

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Global Environmental Protection Act of 1989 and sought a committee hearing on it.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only other senator to support it.

for.name: Subcommittee on Environmental Protection, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on May 19, 1989 (printed as S.Hrg. 101-120), the only committee action it ever received.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (Chair Sen. Quentin Burdick)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, held only a subcommittee hearing, and never reported it out, keeping it from any committee or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nominally bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor and 1 of 45 Republican senators as cosponsor — but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill froze their output at 1987 levels starting in 1990, cut it to 5% by 1994, and banned production entirely by 1996, with mandatory labeling and 99.999% destruction disposal. Their interest ran against the public's, since their products were destroying the ozone layer.

Carbon dioxide limits of 610 pounds per million BTU in 1991, falling to 280 by 2011, and a rule forcing plants to meet new-source standards at 30 years of age, would have forced costly retrofits or retirement of conventional coal plants. The pollution they emit is exactly what the bill targeted.

Tighter tailpipe standards, a 75% carbon dioxide cut by 2011, onboard refueling vapor recovery, a ten-year/100,000-mile emissions warranty, and mandatory defect reporting and recalls raised compliance costs. Cheaper, cleaner-running cars serve the buyers directly.

Low-sulfur diesel (0.05%), summer gasoline vapor-pressure caps, and oxygen-content floors in carbon monoxide areas required refinery investment; small refiners got a reprieve until 1994. Cleaner fuel means less particulate and smog exposure for drivers and people living near roads.

The bill required minimum oxygen content in gasoline sold in carbon monoxide areas and gave 10% ethanol blends a one-pound waiver on gasoline vapor-pressure limits, creating a guaranteed market for ethanol.

The bill set a national goal of 50% of U.S. energy from nonpolluting sources by 2000 and created a commission on inherently safe nuclear reactors, positioning nuclear power to help fill the gap left by constrained fossil generation.
